results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No, creatures phasing back in do not trigger enter the battlefield abilities. Phasing in is not a zone change, and therefore does not trigger abilities that care about permanents entering the battlefield. Enter the battlefield abilities are a type of zone-change trigger [603.6a].

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: When a creature with trample deals combat damage, its controller first assigns damage to any creatures blocking it. Once all blocking creatures have been assigned lethal damage, any excess damage can be assigned to the player, planeswalker, or battle the creature is attacking [702.19b]. Deathtouch means that any amount of damage dealt to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for the purposes of determining excess damage [702.2c]. Therefore, if a creature with trample also has deathtouch, its controller can assign just 1 damage to each blocking creature to destroy them, and then assign any remaining damage to the defending player or planeswalker, as all damage dealt to the blockers would be considered lethal due to deathtouch [702.2c, 702.19b].

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: Yes, you can use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a Commander deck even if only one of the colors in the hybrid symbol is present in the commander's color identity. Therefore, a card with a hybrid mana symbol like {R/G} has both red and green in its color identity. If your commander's color identity is only red, a card with {R/G} in its mana cost would not be allowed in the deck because green is not in the commander's color identity [903.5c]. However, if the card's color identity is only red, and it has a hybrid mana symbol that can be paid with red mana (e.g., {2/R}), it would be allowed. The rule states that each card in a Commander deck must have a color identity that is found within the commander's color identity [903.5c].

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, which means no spells can be cast, no abilities can be activated, and no abilities can resolve during this step. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held until the next time a player would receive priority, which is typically during the upkeep step. The untap step ends when all its specified actions are completed.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. A creature remains an attacking creature until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. The end of combat step is part of the combat phase, and creatures are only removed from combat at the end of that step or if another effect removes them [508.1k, 508.4, 508.4b, 508.4d, 506.4].

results.question: Do you cast lands?

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: No, you cannot sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves. When a creature with Evoke enters the battlefield, its controller sacrifices it if its evoke cost was paid [702.74a]. This sacrifice is part of the process of the creature entering the battlefield, and the triggered ability that causes the sacrifice resolves as part of that process. You cannot sacrifice the creature before this ability resolves because the creature is not yet on the battlefield in a state where it can be sacrificed by another ability or cost. The Evoke ability itself is a triggered ability that occurs when the permanent enters the battlefield [702.74a]. If you sacrifice a creature as part of another cost, such as for an Exploit ability [702.110a], that sacrifice happens when the Exploit ability resolves, which is after the creature has entered the battlefield and the Evoke trigger has already occurred or is on the stack.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes, if a card loses all abilities, that includes its keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are a type of ability that is summarized by a keyword on the card, and effects that remove abilities remove all instances of them. For example, if an effect causes a permanent to lose banding, it also loses all associated "bands with other" abilities.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: You cannot draw cards if you are at your maximum hand size, because you would be required to discard them immediately. The cleanup step includes a turn-based action where a player discards cards from their hand until they reach their maximum hand size [703.4n, 514.1]. If you are already at your maximum hand size, any cards drawn would be excess cards that must be discarded [402.2]. However, if an effect instructs you to draw cards and you have no cards left in your library, you will draw the remaining cards and then lose the game [104.3c].

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker has 0 loyalty, it is put into its owner's graveyard. This is a state-based action, meaning it happens automatically whenever certain conditions are met and does not use the stack. The number of loyalty counters on a planeswalker indicates its loyalty, and a planeswalker with 0 loyalty is subject to this rule. Damage dealt to a planeswalker causes loyalty counters to be removed from it.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No, non-creature artifacts do not die. The term "dies" specifically applies to creatures and planeswalkers being put into a graveyard from the battlefield [Dies]. Rule 701.8b states that only creatures can be destroyed by lethal damage or deathtouch, or by an effect that uses the word "destroy". Other permanents, including artifacts, are not subject to these conditions for dying. Rule 704.5v mentions battles being put into a graveyard, but this is not the same as dying. Rule 310.7 also refers to battles being put into a graveyard. Rule 704.5f refers to creatures with toughness 0 or less being put into a graveyard, and rule 704.5g and 704.5h refer to creatures being destroyed by lethal damage or deathtouch. None of these rules apply to non-creature artifacts.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: If you should draw a card when your library is empty, you draw the remaining cards (which is zero cards) and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. This is a state-based action. If an effect offers you the choice to draw a card when your library is empty, you can choose to do so, and the same game loss condition applies. However, if an effect prevents you from drawing cards, you cannot choose to draw a card even if offered, and thus you do not lose the game for drawing from an empty library in that specific instance.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The steps of the combat phase, in order, are: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. If no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking, the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped [508.8]. There are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike [506.1].

As the defending player, you generally do not receive priority during the combat phase until after the active player has had a chance to act. Specifically, the active player receives priority at the beginning of most steps and phases after turn-based actions are completed [117.3a]. In a two-player game, the nonactive player is the defending player [506.2]. In multiplayer games, the active player chooses one opponent to be the defending player during the beginning of combat step, unless all opponents are automatically defending players [703.4h, 507.1]. If the "Attack Multiple Players Option" is in use, all opponents are defending players [802.2].

You will have priority during the declare blockers step to declare blockers [506.1]. You will also have priority after the combat damage step, during the end of combat step [511.1].

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities do not use the stack, which means they resolve immediately and cannot be responded to, targeted, or countered. This applies to both activated and triggered mana abilities. [605.3b], [113.4], [605.4a], [405.6c]

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a cost being paid. Costs are paid as part of casting a spell or activating an ability, and once the total cost is determined, it becomes "locked in" and cannot be changed by effects that would alter it. The process of casting a spell involves determining and paying costs [601.2g]. Mana abilities can be activated before costs are paid [118.2], [601.2g], [508.1i], [509.1e]. However, once the player begins paying the costs, they must pay the full amount, as partial payments are not allowed [508.1j], [509.1f], [118.3]. If a player is unable to complete the payment of costs, the casting of the spell or activation of the ability is illegal, and the game returns to the moment before the action was proposed [601.2g], [508.1j], [509.1f].

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
The layer system is a method used in Magic: The Gathering to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to an object's characteristics [Layer]. This system ensures that effects are applied in a consistent and predictable manner, even when multiple effects modify the same characteristic. The process begins with the object's base characteristics, and then applies continuous effects in a series of layers and sublayers [613.1]. Within each layer and sublayer, effects are generally applied in timestamp order, meaning earlier effects are applied before later ones [613.7]. However, dependencies between effects can override the timestamp order [613.8].

The layers are as follows:

*   **Layer 1:** Rules and effects that modify copiable values are applied. This includes copy effects and effects that set power and toughness when an object enters the battlefield or is turned face up [613.1a, 613.2a]. The result of this layer determines the object's copiable values [613.2c].
*   **Layer 2:** Control-changing effects are applied [613.3].
*   **Layer 3:** Text-changing effects are applied [613.1c].
*   **Layer 4:** Type-changing effects are applied, including changes to card types, subtypes, and supertypes [613.1d].
*   **Layer 5:** Color-changing effects are applied [613.1e].
*   **Layer 6:** Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that prevent an object from having an ability are applied [613.1f].
*   **Layer 7:** Power- and toughness-changing effects are applied. This layer has several sublayers:
    *   **Layer 7a:** Effects from characteristic-defining abilities that define power and/or toughness [613.4a].
    *   **Layer 7b:** Other power- and toughness-setting effects [613.6].
    *   **Layer 7c:** Power- and toughness-modifying effects, such as those from +1/+1 counters or spells that grant bonuses [613.5].

An effect that spans multiple layers, such as one that changes a creature's color and also grants it a power and toughness bonus, will have its parts applied in the appropriate layers [613.6].

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action that applies when a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name. When this occurs, that player must choose one of those permanents to keep, and all the others are put into their owners' graveyards. This rule applies to any permanent with the supertype "legendary." Older planeswalker cards have received errata to have the legendary supertype, making them subject to the legend rule.

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text: Your creature dies as a state-based action after it has been marked with lethal damage. State-based actions are checked and performed automatically whenever a player would receive priority, or during the cleanup step. If a creature has damage marked on it equal to or greater than its toughness, it is destroyed as a state-based action. This happens before any player receives priority. Damage marked on a creature remains until the cleanup step, even if it stops being a creature. However, if the creature regenerates, this can prevent it from being destroyed. The game checks for state-based actions, including creatures with lethal damage, before a player gets priority [117.5]. If any state-based actions are performed, the check is repeated. Once no more state-based actions are performed, the player who would have received priority does so [704.3]. Damage is also removed during the cleanup step [514.2].

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: Yes, you can cast your commander from exile, provided it is a Commander game. Rule [903.9] states that a commander may return to the command zone during a Commander game. Specifically, rule [903.9a] clarifies that if a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. This is a state-based action. Rule [704.6d] also mentions this for Commander games. Additionally, rule [903.3d] and [903.3e] define what a commander is and that it retains its designation even when changing zones. Rule [601.3f] and [406.3b] discuss casting spells from exile, which would apply if your commander is in exile and you are casting it from there.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text: During the cleanup step, the active player first discards cards if their hand size exceeds the maximum. Then, all damage marked on permanents is removed, and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end. These actions happen simultaneously and do not use the stack. Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, meaning no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated. However, if state-based actions need to be performed or triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, those actions are performed, the abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player receives priority. If no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, the cleanup step ends without players receiving priority.

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: State-based actions are checked throughout the game whenever a player would get priority, and also during the cleanup step. They are performed automatically when certain conditions are met and do not use the stack. State-based actions are dealt with before a player would receive priority. If any state-based actions are performed, the check is repeated until no more state-based actions are performed. State-based actions are also checked when an effect ends the combat phase or ends the turn, before any triggered abilities are put onto the stack and before any player receives priority.

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: A player can concede the game at any time. When a player concedes, they leave the game immediately and lose the game. This is true even if that player is controlled by another player, or if they are playing in a Two-Headed Giant game where their team will lose the game. The ability for a player to concede at any time is an exception that overrides other rules.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is the player whose turn it is [102.1]. In games using the shared team turns option, the active team is the team whose turn it is, and each player on that team is considered an active player for the purpose of making choices [805.4a].

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When a player who is not the active player casts a spell, that player receives priority first. This is because casting a spell is an action that grants priority to the player who performed it, according to rule [117.3c].

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When the active player casts a spell, that player receives priority afterward. This is because the active player is the one casting the spell, and rule [117.3c] states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. This is an exception to the general rule that the active player receives priority after a spell resolves, as stated in rule [117.3b].

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: You can hold priority to cast more spells after casting one or more spells if you have priority after the first spell resolves. Normally, after a spell or ability resolves, the active player receives priority [117.3b]. If you cast a spell, you receive priority afterward if you had priority before casting it [117.3c]. However, if a spell or ability instructs a player to cast another spell during its resolution, no player receives priority after the second spell is cast [608.2g].

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text: Lore counters are put on Sagas in two main ways. First, when a Saga enters the battlefield, it may enter with lore counters. If the Saga has read ahead, its controller chooses a number between one and the final chapter number, and the Saga enters with that many lore counters [714.3b]. This is a turn-based action and does not use the stack [703.4f, 505.4].

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect that does something later in the game, rather than when the spell or ability that created it resolves [603.7]. These abilities typically contain the words "when," "whenever," or "at," though these words may not begin the ability itself [603.7]. They are created during the resolution of spells or abilities, as a result of a replacement effect being applied, or from a static ability that allows a player to take an action [603.7a]. A delayed triggered ability will only trigger the next time its trigger event occurs, unless it has a stated duration [603.7b]. If a spell creates a delayed triggered ability, that spell is its source, and the player who controlled the spell as it resolved is its controller [603.7d]. If an activated or triggered ability creates a delayed triggered ability, the source and controller are the same as the original ability [603.7e]. If a static ability generates a replacement effect that creates a delayed triggered ability, the object with the static ability is the source, and the controller is the player who controlled that object when the replacement effect was applied [603.7f]. If a static ability allows a player to take an action and creates a delayed triggered ability if they do, the object with the static ability is the source, and the controller is the player who controlled that object when the action was taken [603.7g]. A delayed triggered ability refers to a particular object even if it changes characteristics, but it won't affect the object if it's no longer in the expected zone when the ability resolves [603.7c]. If a delayed triggered ability refers to X, and X was chosen for the cost of the spell or ability that created it, the value of X for the triggered ability is the same [107.3n]. A delayed triggered ability is put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3a].

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells can have abilities. Abilities of an instant or sorcery spell, which are non-permanent spells, usually function while that object is on the stack [113.6]. Spell abilities are defined as abilities followed as instructions while an instant or sorcery spell is resolving [113.3a]. results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text: Monastery Swiftspear's prowess ability triggers when you cast Shardless Agent, and it resolves before the spell that Shardless Agent's cascade ability puts onto the stack. results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. When a manifested permanent that is represented by an instant or sorcery card would be exiled, it is put into its owner's graveyard instead. results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?

The exiled creature will return when Banishing Light phases back in.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?

Therefore, if Emrakul, the Promised End is countered, its cast trigger will not occur, and you will not gain control of your opponent's next turn.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text: Yes, Valki, God of Lies is a legal cascade hit because it is a nonland card. However, you cannot cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side for free. Cascade requires that the exiled card's mana value be less than the cascade spell's mana value, and that the resulting spell's mana value also be less than the cascade spell's mana value [702.85a]. When casting a double-faced card, its front face is used by default [712.11c]. The front face of Valki, God of Lies has a mana value of 2 ({1}{B}). If your cascade spell has a mana value greater than 2, you can cast Valki, God of Lies for free. However, the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face has a mana value of 7 ({5}{B}{R}). Even if you could cast the Tibalt face, its mana value of 7 is not less than the mana value of Valki, God of Lies (2), which is the mana value used for determining if the cascade hit is legal [712.8c]. Therefore, you can only cast the Valki, God of Lies face for free, not the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text: You will control your opponent's next turn once, and you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End. Copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell with Lithoform Engine does not give you another control-a-turn trigger. The cast trigger of Emrakul, the Promised End is a triggered ability, and Lithoform Engine's ability to copy a permanent spell creates a copy of the spell itself, not its triggered abilities. The first copy of the Emrakul, the Promised End trigger is created by Lithoform Engine's ability to copy an activated or triggered ability [Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. This trigger targets an opponent and causes you to gain control of that opponent's next turn [Emrakul, the Promised End]. The second Emrakul, the Promised End is a copy of the permanent spell, created by Lithoform Engine's ability to copy a permanent spell [Lithoform Engine ruling #5]. This copy becomes a token when it resolves [111.13]. The cast trigger of Emrakul, the Promised End does not trigger again when the copy of the spell resolves because the copy is not cast [707.10b]. The rule states that a copy of a spell is not cast [707.10b]. The first Emrakul, the Promised End's cast trigger targets an opponent, and you gain control of that opponent's next turn. The extra turn granted by the original Emrakul, the Promised End will occur after that controlled turn [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #16]. If multiple player-controlling effects affect the same player, the last one created is the one that works [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. In this scenario, only one such effect is created.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you will get two tokens. When you activate Mimic Vat's ability, you are creating a token that is a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat. This ability is put onto the stack. Then, you use Lithoform Engine's ability to copy that activated ability. This puts a second copy of the Mimic Vat ability onto the stack. When the first copy of the Mimic Vat ability resolves, it will create a token that is a copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat at that time. Then, when the second copy of the Mimic Vat ability resolves, it will create another token that is a copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat at that time. This results in two tokens being created. Rule [707.10] states that a copy of an ability copies the characteristics of the original ability. Rule [707.10e] further clarifies that if an effect copies a spell or ability, and that copy targets an object, the copy targets that object. In this case, both copies of the Mimic Vat ability will target the same exiled card, and thus create two tokens. Rule [607.3] is relevant if there were multiple cards exiled with Mimic Vat, but in this scenario, it is assumed there is one card exiled.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text: If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0 while your opponent controls an untapped Trinisphere and you have a permanent that reduces your green spells by {1}, the spell will cost {1}{G}{G} to cast. You will create zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens. To cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, you should choose X=0. The process of casting a spell begins with proposing the spell and determining its costs [601.2a]. The total cost is determined by starting with the mana cost or alternative cost, adding any cost increases, and then applying cost reductions [601.2f]. For Awaken the Woods, the mana cost is {X}{G}{G}. If X=0, the mana cost is {G}{G}. Your permanent reduces the cost of your green spells by {1}, so the cost becomes {G}. However, Trinisphere states that spells that would cost less than three mana to cast cost three mana to cast, as long as Trinisphere is untapped [Trinisphere ruling #0]. Since {G} is less than three mana, Trinisphere increases the cost to {3}. The mana component of the total cost is then {1}{G}{G} [Trinisphere ruling #0]. You will create zero tokens because X=0 [Awaken the Woods card text]. To cast Awaken the Woods for a value greater than zero, you would need to choose a higher value for X. For example, if you chose X=1, the mana cost would be {1}{G}{G}. Your permanent would reduce this to {G}{G}. Trinisphere would then increase this to {3}, resulting in a total cost of {1}{G}{G} [Trinisphere ruling #0].

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard to the battlefield with Animate Dead. When Animate Dead resolves, it will return Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control and attach itself to Grist, the Hunger Tide. Because Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card in your graveyard, it can be targeted by Animate Dead. According to rule [400.7], an object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of its previous existence. However, Grist, the Hunger Tide has an exception to this rule: "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types." This means that even though Grist, the Hunger Tide is a planeswalker card, it is also a creature card while in your graveyard, making it a legal target for Animate Dead. When Grist, the Hunger Tide enters the battlefield, it will be a planeswalker, and the enchantment effect of Animate Dead will attach to it. The enchanted creature, Grist, the Hunger Tide, gets -1/-0. If Animate Dead leaves the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide's controller will sacrifice it.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave does not keep its counters when it moves to the command zone. When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies, it moves from the battlefield to the graveyard. Rule [122.2] states that counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another. Therefore, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave loses its four +1/+1 counters when it moves to the graveyard. Rule [903.9b] allows a commander to return to the command zone instead of its owner's hand or library. However, this rule does not apply when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is put into the graveyard. When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is recast, it enters the battlefield as a new object. Rule [400.7] states that an object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. If you control Doubling Season, it will double any counters that are put onto Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it enters the battlefield, as per Doubling Season ruling [Doubling Season ruling #2] and rule [616.1f]. However, since Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is entering the battlefield with no counters, Doubling Season will have no effect on it.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game. When you activate Sundial of the Infinite's ability, it ends the current turn. This process skips the end step and proceeds directly to the cleanup step [724.1d]. Because the end step is skipped, the triggered ability from Final Fortune that causes you to lose the game at the beginning of that turn's end step does not trigger [724.1e]. According to the rulings for Final Fortune, if you skip the extra turn gained, you do not lose the game [Final Fortune ruling #1].

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: When you cast Clone, you choose what it copies as it enters the battlefield, not when you cast it. This choice is part of the process of Clone entering the battlefield. Your opponent can respond to the spell Clone after you cast it, but before it enters the battlefield. They cannot respond to the choice of what Clone copies because that choice is made as it enters the battlefield, which is after the spell has resolved and is no longer on the stack. Clone's ability does not target the chosen creature [Clone ruling #0]. If Clone enters the battlefield at the same time as another creature, Clone cannot become a copy of that creature; you may only choose a creature that is already on the battlefield [Clone ruling #2]. If you choose not to copy anything, Clone enters as a 0/0 Shapeshifter creature and is likely put into the graveyard immediately [Clone ruling #5].

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text: You will get one land from that one Flooded Strand. When you activate Flooded Strand's ability, you search your library for a Plains or Island card and put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle your library. Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability copies an activated or triggered ability that is on the stack [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. In this case, the ability being copied is the search ability of Flooded Strand. Gogo's ability creates copies of the ability on the stack, and these copies are treated as separate instances of the ability [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. However, rule [701.23h] states that if an effect instructs a player to search a library more than once before instructing a player to shuffle that library, it is the same as a single instruction to search that library for all those cards, and the player searches that library only once. Therefore, even though Gogo creates two copies of the Flooded Strand's search ability, you will only search your library once and thus only get one land.
